authored_explainer.title: Cereal Production Is 1.5x Higher Than In 1972
authored_explainer.hook: The 1970s warned of food shortages; cereal production rose 1.5x instead.
says: In 1985, secondary-school progression was 77.8%. By 2017, it reached 91.3%—1.2 times higher, widening the path beyond primary school.
Cereal production rose from 1083.7 million metric tons in 1972 to 1644.1 million in 2024—1.5 times higher, feeding a larger world.
China leads farmland at 5.2 million square kilometers; the United States has 4.2, Australia 3.6, Brazil 2.4, and Russia 2.2.
authored_explainer.closing: Food shortages did not vanish, but higher output changed how many people the world can feed.
authored_explainer.question: Which surprised you: school, grain, or land?

authored_explainer.title: Combustible Renewables And Waste Is 3.0x Higher Than In 1990
authored_explainer.hook: Since 1990, waste-based energy tripled—without being solar or wind.
says: In 1990, combustible renewables and waste supplied 10.2% of energy. By 2024, 30.1%—3.0 times higher—showing discarded material became major fuel.
Electricity access rose from 73.2% in 1998 to 91.9% by 2024—1.3 times higher, bringing power to far more people.
Waste methane emissions climbed from 903.8 Mt CO2e in 1972 to 1,652 Mt CO2e by 2024—1.8 times higher, raising the climate cost.
authored_explainer.closing: Waste supplies nearly a third of energy, but rising methane keeps the climate bill open.
authored_explainer.question: Which surprised you: fuel, power, or waste?

authored_explainer.title: Population Growth Fell 54% Since 1972
authored_explainer.hook: Population growth was meant to keep accelerating. It fell 54% instead.
says: Rural population fell from 63.1% in 1972 to 42.2% in 2025—down to 67 percent of that, as people shifted toward cities.
Largest-city population barely moved: 18.2% of urban residents in 1972 versus 16.2% in 2025, so urban growth spread beyond one center.
Population growth dropped from 2 annual % in 1972 to 0.91 annual % in 2025—down to 46 percent of that, reshaping future demand.
authored_explainer.closing: Slower growth changes how communities plan schools, homes, jobs, and care.
authored_explainer.question: Which surprised you: rural, city, or growth?
